claim: AWS recommends an Application Load Balancer when you need to load balance HTTP requests or need flexible application management.
q: Which load balancer does AWS recommend for HTTP requests and flexible application management?
values: If you need to load balance HTTP requests
If you need flexible application management
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/faqs
If you need to load balance HTTP requests, we recommend you use the Application Load Balancer (ALB).
www/elasticloadbalancing/features
If you need flexible application management, we recommend that you use an Application Load Balancer.

claim: AWS recommends a Network Load Balancer for layer 4 (TCP, UDP) load balancing, for extreme performance and low latency, and when the application needs a static IP.
q: Which load balancer does AWS recommend for TCP or UDP traffic, extreme performance, or a static IP?
values: extreme performance and static IP is needed
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/faqs
For network/transport protocols (layer4 – TCP, UDP) load balancing, and for extreme performance/low latency applications we recommend using Network Load Balancer.
www/elasticloadbalancing/features
If extreme performance and static IP is needed for your application, we recommend that you use a Network Load Balancer.

claim: AWS says to use a Gateway Load Balancer when you need to deploy and run third-party virtual appliances.
q: Which load balancer type does AWS name for deploying and running third-party virtual appliances?
values: you can use Gateway Load Balancer
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/faqs
If you need to deploy and run third-party virtual appliances, you can use Gateway Load Balancer.

claim: In the AWS product comparison, an Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, a Network Load Balancer at layer 4, a Gateway Load Balancer as a layer 3 gateway with layer 4 load balancing, and a Classic Load Balancer at layer 4/7.
q: At which OSI layer does each Elastic Load Balancing load balancer type work?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| Load Balancer type | Layer 7 | Layer 4 | Layer 3 Gateway + Layer 4 Load Balancing | Layer 4/7 |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |

claim: In the AWS product comparison, Application Load Balancer listeners use HTTP, HTTPS and gRPC, Network Load Balancer listeners use TCP, UDP and TLS, and a Gateway Load Balancer listens for IP traffic.
q: Which listener protocols does each load balancer type use in the AWS product comparison?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| Protocol listeners | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC | TCP, UDP, TLS | IP | TCP, SSL/TLS, HTTP, HTTPS |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |

claim: In the AWS product comparison, an Application Load Balancer targets IP addresses, instances and Lambda functions; a Network Load Balancer targets IP addresses, instances and an Application Load Balancer; a Gateway Load Balancer targets IP addresses and instances.
q: Which target types does each load balancer type support in the AWS product comparison?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| Target type | IP, Instance, Lambda | IP, Instance, Application Load Balancer | IP, Instance | - |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |

claim: In the AWS product comparison, Application and Network Load Balancers are reached through a virtual IP (VIP), while a Gateway Load Balancer is reached through a route table entry and does not terminate the flow.
q: How is traffic sent to a Gateway Load Balancer, compared with an Application or Network Load Balancer?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| Reachable via | VIP | VIP | Route table entry | - |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |
www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| Terminates flow/proxy behavior | Yes | Yes | No | Yes |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |

claim: In the AWS feature table, only the Network Load Balancer has a static or Elastic IP address; the Application, Gateway and Classic Load Balancers do not.
q: Which load balancer type offers a static or Elastic IP address?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| IP address - Static, Elastic | - | ✔ | - | - |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |

claim: In the AWS feature table, user authentication is a feature of the Application Load Balancer only.
q: Which load balancer type can authenticate users?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| User Authentication | ✔ | - | - | - |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |

claim: In the AWS feature table, Application, Network and Classic Load Balancers support security groups and SSL offloading; a Gateway Load Balancer supports neither.
q: Which load balancer types support security groups and SSL offloading?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| Security Groups | ✔ | ✔ | - | ✔ |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |
www/elasticloadbalancing/features
| SSL Offloading | ✔ | ✔ | - | ✔ |
| Feature | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer | Gateway Load Balancer | Classic Load Balancer |

claim: To give Application Load Balancer layer 7 routing a static IP address or AWS PrivateLink, you forward traffic from a Network Load Balancer to an Application Load Balancer-type target group that holds the Application Load Balancer.
q: How can an application that needs Application Load Balancer routing also get static IP addresses or PrivateLink?
values: forward traffic from your Network Load Balancer
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/application-load-balancer-target

You can use the layer 7 request-based routing feature of the Application Load Balancer in combination with features that the Network Load Balancer supports, such as endpoint services (AWS PrivateLink) and static IP addresses.
www/elasticloadbalancing/faqs
You can forward traffic from your Network Load Balancer, which provides support for PrivateLink and a static IP address per Availability Zone, to your Application Load Balancer.

claim: To register an Application Load Balancer as a target of a Network Load Balancer, both load balancers must be in the same VPC in the same account.
q: Where must an Application Load Balancer be to become the target of a Network Load Balancer?
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/application-load-balancer-target
To associate an Application Load Balancer as a target of a Network Load Balancer, the load balancers must be in the same VPC within the same account.

claim: One Application Load Balancer can be the target of up to two Network Load Balancers, with a separate target group for each Network Load Balancer.
q: How many Network Load Balancers can use the same Application Load Balancer as a target?
values: up to two Network Load Balancers
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/application-load-balancer-target
You can associate an Application Load Balancer as a target of up to two Network Load Balancers.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/application-load-balancer-target
To do this, register the Application Load Balancer with a separate target group for each Network Load Balancer.

claim: Endpoints of a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator can be Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers, EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses; the accelerator's static IP addresses are the single point of contact for clients.
q: Which load balancer types can be endpoints of a Global Accelerator standard accelerator?
values: Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers
a single point of contact for clients
ev: docs/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints
Endpoints for standard accelerators in AWS Global Accelerator can be Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers, Amazon EC2 instances, or Elastic IP addresses.
docs/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints

In AWS Global Accelerator, static IP addresses serve as a single point of contact for clients, and, with a standard accelerator, Global Accelerator distributes incoming traffic across healthy endpoints.

claim: With host conditions, one Application Load Balancer can route requests for multiple domains, based on the host field in the HTTP header.
q: How can one Application Load Balancer serve several domains?
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction
You can configure rules for your listener that forward requests based on the host field in the HTTP header.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction
This enables you to route requests to multiple domains using a single load balancer.

claim: With path conditions, an Application Load Balancer forwards requests based on the URL, so you can split an application into smaller services and route each request to the correct service.
q: How does an Application Load Balancer route requests to different services of one application?
values: forward requests based on the URL
structure your application as smaller services
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction
You can configure rules for your listener that forward requests based on the URL in the request.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction
This enables you to structure your application as smaller services, and route requests to the correct service based on the content of the URL.

claim: An Application Load Balancer can route to multiple applications on one EC2 instance: you register the instance or IP address with several target groups, each on a different port.
q: How can one Application Load Balancer reach several applications that run on the same instance?
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction
You can register an instance or IP address with multiple target groups, each on a different port.

claim: An Application Load Balancer is charged for each hour or partial hour that it is running, and each partial hour is billed as a full hour, plus the Load Balancer Capacity Units (LCU) it uses.
q: Does an Application Load Balancer bill per hour even when little traffic flows, and how is a partial hour billed?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You are charged for each hour or partial hour that an Application Load Balancer is running.
www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
Each partial Application Load Balancer hour used is billed as a full hour.
www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You are also charged for the number of Load Balancer Capacity Units (LCU) used per minute.

claim: A Network Load Balancer and a Gateway Load Balancer are each charged for every hour or partial hour they run, with each partial hour billed as a full hour, plus the capacity units they use (NLCU or GLCU).
q: How are Network Load Balancers and Gateway Load Balancers billed for running time?
scope: per Network Load Balancer or Gateway Load Balancer
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You are charged for each hour or partial hour that a Network Load Balancer is running.
www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
Each partial Network Load Balancer hour used is billed as a full hour.
www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You are charged for each hour or partial hour that a Gateway Load Balancer is running.
www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You are also charged for the number of Network Load Balancer Capacity Units (NLCU) used by Network Load Balancer per minute.
www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You are also charged for the number of Gateway Load Balancer Capacity Units (GLCU) used by Gateway Load Balancer per minute.

claim: For an Application Load Balancer with 10 or fewer rules, the rule evaluations dimension is ignored in the LCU calculation, so many routing rules on one load balancer only add cost above 10 rules.
q: When does the number of listener rules start to add LCU cost on an Application Load Balancer?
scope: per Application Load Balancer, LCU rule evaluations dimension
cond: rules configured on the load balancer
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
Note 2: If you have 10 or fewer rules configured, the rule evaluations dimension is ignored in LCU computation.

claim: On top of the load balancer charges, you pay standard AWS data transfer charges and standard public IPv4 address charges for all addresses your load balancers consume.
q: Which charges come on top of the Elastic Load Balancing hourly and capacity unit charges?
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You will incur standard AWS data transfer charges, in addition to any ELB charges.
www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
You will incur standard public IPv4 address charges for all the addresses you consume with load balancers.

claim: The Gateway Load Balancer endpoint (GWLBE), a VPC endpoint type powered by AWS PrivateLink, is priced and billed separately from the Gateway Load Balancer.
q: Is the Gateway Load Balancer endpoint included in the Gateway Load Balancer price?
values: GWLBE is priced and billed separately
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
GWLBE is priced and billed separately.

claim: You are not charged for traffic that the inbound security group rules of a Network Load Balancer block.
q: Do you pay for traffic that a Network Load Balancer security group blocks?
values: You are not charged for traffic
blocked by inbound security group rules
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-security-groups
You are not charged for traffic that is blocked by inbound security group rules.

claim: You can associate security groups with a Network Load Balancer only when you create it; if you create it without security groups, you cannot add them later, so AWS recommends adding one at creation.
q: Can you add a security group to an existing Network Load Balancer that was created without one?
values: can't associate them with the Network Load Balancer
We recommend that you associate a security group
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-security-groups
If you create a Network Load Balancer without associating any security groups, you can't associate them with the Network Load Balancer later on.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-security-groups
We recommend that you associate a security group with your Network Load Balancer when you create it.

claim: If a Network Load Balancer has no security group, all client traffic can reach its listeners and all traffic can leave it.
q: What traffic can reach a Network Load Balancer that has no security group?
values: all traffic can leave the Network Load Balancer
scope: Network Load Balancer without a security group
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-security-groups
If you don't assign a security group to your Network Load Balancer, all client traffic can reach the Network Load Balancer listeners and all traffic can leave the Network Load Balancer.

claim: If the target security groups allow traffic only from the security group of the Network Load Balancer, clients can reach the targets through the load balancer but not directly.
q: How do you stop clients from bypassing a Network Load Balancer and reaching its targets directly?
values: prevents them from sending traffic directly
scope: Network Load Balancer and its targets
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-security-groups

You can add a rule to the security groups associated with your targets that references the security group associated with your Network Load Balancer. This allows clients to send traffic to your targets through your Network Load Balancer, but prevents them from sending traffic directly to your targets.
